study.title: BOLT: Imaging Lightning and Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes at the Pierre Auger Observatory

cover.headline: A new detector array could help explain **how lightning produces rare bursts of gamma rays** visible from space.

slides.title: If this imaging system works, it may let scientists watch the exact moment a lightning bolt creates high-energy radiation.
slides.body:
Terrestrial gamma-ray flashes are rare bursts of radiation linked to the start of lightning. Researchers still don't know how they form.

The team is building BOLT, a radio array that maps lightning in 3D alongside detectors that have already caught gamma flashes.

slides.title: The BOLT array uses radio detectors sensitive to frequencies between 30 MHz and 80 MHz to image lightning propagation.
slides.body:
The team reports that the array is now in commissioning. Station firmware has been modified to capture and stream multi-second waveforms.

The system sits at Pierre Auger Observatory, which has already recorded signals tied to gamma-ray flashes.

slides.title: BOLT builds on VHF radio detectors originally developed for the Auger Engineering Radio Array.
slides.body:
VHF stands for very high frequency radio waves. These detectors map where and when lightning emits radio signals as it branches through a storm.

By matching that 3D picture to gamma-ray signals, the team hopes to pinpoint which part of a discharge goes with the flash.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has verified the work yet.
This paper describes a system still in commissioning. The array has not yet produced the coincidence measurements it was built to capture.
This study found a pattern linking gamma-ray flashes to lightning. That does not show one causes the other.
The implications on slide one are our extrapolation of what this tool may enable, not a claim the authors make in the abstract.

source.abstract: Lightning-related phenomena are known to interact with and influence all detector systems of the Pierre Auger Observatory. Notably, the Surface Detector has recorded unique signals associated with Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes (TGFs), which are rare phenomena linked to the initial processes of lightning. Studying TGFs in coincidence with their parent lightning discharges helps to constrain the mechanisms responsible for their production, providing key insights into how these high-energy emissions are generated and evolve within thunderstorms. To image the parent lightning discharges, we are developing the Broadband Observatory of Lightning and TGFs (BOLT), an interferometric lightning mapping array that enhances the unique capabilities of the Observatory by providing high-resolution 3D (spatial and temporal) imaging of lightning propagation. BOLT consists of VHF radio detectors that have been previously developed for the Auger Engineering Radio Array, sensitive in the 30 MHz to 80 MHz range. The array is co-located with the Surface Detector to enable direct correlation between lightning activity and candidate TGF signals at the Pierre Auger Observatory. The BOLT array is in commissioning, with successful station firmware modifications to acquire and stream multi-second waveforms.
